DECISION 
 
1. 
The appeals are allowed.  
 
2. 
The panel determined that the council tax valuation list entries for the appeal properties 
should be reduced from band G to band F with effect from their respective dates of entry into 
the council tax list, as set out in the Schedule on page two. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
On 29 and 30 April 2025, Mr Van Loen, on behalf of the appellants, served proposals on the 
Listing Officer (LO) on the basis that the entries for each property did not take into account a 
relevant decision of a local Valuation Tribunal, namely the decision dated 16 October 2024 in 
respect of 12 Caves Gardens, MK43 0TP (VT00020674). In making the proposals, the 
appellants sought a reduction in the valuation list entry from band G to band F. After 
considering the merits of the proposals, the LO determined that they were not well founded 
and decision notices to this effect were issued on 23 January 2026.  
 
4. 
The appeals, received on 27 February 2026, were made to the Valuation Tribunal for 
England under regulation 10 of the Council Tax (Alteration of Lists and Appeals) (England) 
Regulations 2009. 
 
5. 
At Mr Van Loen’s request, and with the permission of the panel, the nine appeals were heard 
together as they raised substantially the same valuation issues and relied on largely identical 
evidence. Prior to the hearing, the LO filed joint evidence bundles in respect of the nine 
appeals, containing contributions from the appellants and the LO, as required by the 
Tribunal’s standard directions. The LO also stated that copies of the judgments of Domblides 
v Listing Officer [2008] EWHC 3271 (Admin) and Ladies Hosiery & Underwear Ltd v 
Middlesex Assessment Committee (1932) had been provided to the appellants’ 
representative. 
 
6. 
This statement of reasons is not and does not purport to be a full verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Issue 
 
7. 
The panel had to decide which council tax band the appeal properties should be placed in. 
 
Relevant Law 
 
8. 
Regulation 6 of the Council Tax (Situation and Valuation of Dwellings) Regulations 1992 (SI 
1992 No. 550) sets out the statutory basis for valuing dwellings for the purposes of their entry 
into the valuation list. It provides that, having regard to the statutory assumptions, the value 
of any dwelling, shall be taken to be the amount it would reasonably expect to realise had it 
been sold in an open market by a willing vendor, on the antecedent valuation date of 1 April 
1991. 
 
9. 
Section 5(2) of the Local Government Finance Act 1992 sets out the eight valuation bands to 
which dwellings in England are allocated. The bands provide the 1991 range of values. In 
this case, the appeal properties were entered in valuation band G, which applies to values

4/7 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
above £160,000 but no more than £320,000. The appellants sought reductions to band F, 
which applies to values above £120,000 but no more than £160,000. 
 
10. In deciding the values that would have been achieved on 1 April 1991, consideration had to 
be given to the physical state of the locality and the size, layout and character of the 
dwellings on their respective relevant dates, being the dates on which the appeal properties 
entered the valuation list. 
 
Discussion 
 
11. The appeal properties were all five-bedroom detached houses in Marston Moretaine built by 
David Wilson Homes. Their accommodation comprised a lounge, dining room, study, kitchen 
and family room, utility room and cloakroom on the ground floor, with five bedrooms, two en-
suite shower rooms and a family bathroom on the first floor. Numbers 6 Little Blakelands, 10 
Little Beanhills and 21 Great Blakelands were constructed in 2014 and were the “Manning” 
house type, measuring 227m². The “Glidewell” properties comprised 27 Busby Mead, 11 
Huckle Green, 11 and 15 Harrison Meadow and 5 Harper Grove. They measured 237m² and 
were constructed later, between 2018 and 2024. Number 17 Great Blakelands was originally 
a Manning house but was extended from 227m² to 257m². It contained an additional 
reception room, giving it four living rooms rather than three. All nine properties also benefited 
from double garages. 
 
12. The panel was, in essence, required to consider the open market value of the properties as 
at 1 April 1991 and considered that the best evidence was to be found in the sales of similar 
properties in the locality close to the valuation date. This baseline date is established by 
legislation and is applicable to all properties, including those that have been built after that 
date.  
 
13. None of the appeal properties were in existence on 1 April 1991. Therefore, it was 
reasonable to value them having regard to other detached houses that were comparable and 
which had sold around 1991. The closer the properties were in terms of size, location and 
accommodation, the better the evidence. 
 
14. In support of band G, Mr Snell presented the sales of seven smaller detached houses in 
band F that had sold close to 1 April 1991. Four of those properties measured between 
142m² and 179m² and sold for values towards the upper end of band F within a year of the 
antecedent valuation date. However, they were located in Wootton, Cranfield and Ampthill, 
between 2 and 3 miles from the appeal properties. The panel considered that they were too 
far from the appeal properties to provide reliable evidence of values within Marston 
Moretaine and it therefore placed little weight upon them. 
 
15. The panel attached greater weight to the sales of 3, 11 and 14 Denbigh Close because those 
properties were within Marston Moretaine and had sold close to 1 April 1991. They were four-
bedroom detached houses measuring 151m². Number 3 sold for £148,000 in September 
1990, number 14 sold for £153,500 in September 1990 and number 11 sold for £130,000 in 
December 1991. The parties agreed that these sales showed a fall in the market between 
late 1990 and late 1991. They also broadly agreed that the evidence indicated a value in the 
region of £138,000 to £140,000 at the antecedent valuation date. The panel noted that the 
two higher sales occurred before the market had fallen to the level shown by the December 
1991 sale.

16. The panel accepted that the appeal properties would have been more valuable than the 
Denbigh Close properties. However, it was difficult to determine whether the difference would 
have been sufficient to produce values above £160,000. The Denbigh Close properties 
measured 151m², whereas the appeal properties measured between 227m² and 257m². This 
substantial difference in size made it difficult to make a direct comparison. The panel was not 
persuaded that the difference in floor area, by itself, showed how much more the appeal 
properties would have sold for in 1991. No sale of a similar-sized band G property in Marston 
Moretaine close to 1 April 1991 was presented to confirm that the appeal properties would 
have exceeded the band F upper limit. 
 
17. The LO sought to support its valuation by applying percentage differences in floor area and 
later sale prices to the Denbigh Close evidence. The 2017 sale of 14 Denbigh Close for 
£430,000 was compared with the 2017 sale of 21 Great Blakelands for £590,000 and the LO 
also relied upon the higher later sale prices achieved by other appeal properties. 
 
18. However, the panel was not satisfied that applying a percentage difference in size or later 
sale price to a 1990 or 1991 sale provided a sufficiently reliable valuation method. Size was 
relevant, but it was not the only factor affecting value. The evidence did not establish that the 
same percentage differences would have applied in the local market on 1 April 1991. The 
panel therefore placed some weight upon the LO’s sales evidence but did not consider that it 
established values above £160,000 for the appeal properties. 
 
19. The panel also had regard to the ‘tone’ or pattern of bandings already in the valuation list. A 
tone of band was established when a number of properties, similar in size, character, quality, 
detachment and location were attributed the same level of band which, over time, had not 
been challenged. Council tax bands that had been challenged and subsequently agreed by 
parties, or determined by a tribunal panel, were also instrumental in establishing the tone. 
 
20. When the original valuation list was compiled in 1993, a tone had not been established as 
many of the initial bandings were being challenged.  However, the bands were now in a more 
settled stage in the life of the valuation list after over 30 years of scrutiny. It was therefore 
reasonable to place some reliance on this evidence. 
 
21. To further support the appellants’ case, Mr Van Loen provided the panel with the previous 
Tribunal decision of 8 Huckle Green (VT00012229), which was the relevant decision that 
formed the basis of appeal for 12 Caves Gardens. At 237m², it was also a five-bedroom 
detached house situated within Marston Moretaine, and its entry had been reduced from 
band G to band F. The panel also noted that it had virtually the same level of accommodation 
and was the same size as five of the appeal properties. 
 
22. The proposals giving rise to these appeals were based on the Tribunal decision dated 16 
October 2024 concerning 12 Caves Gardens, Marston Moretaine MK43 0TP (VT00020674). 
That property was a five-bedroom detached house measuring 213m², with a double garage, 
and its entry had been reduced from band G to band F. 
 
23. The panel was aware that previous Valuation Tribunal decisions were not binding upon it, but 
they could assist in determining the value or tone of properties within the same locality. Both 
decisions concerned modern five-bedroom detached houses within Marston Moretaine and 
therefore carried significant persuasive weight. The panel also noted that, following the 
decision concerning 12 Caves Gardens, the LO had reduced a substantial number of other 
properties from band G to band F. Those reductions contributed to the current tone of the list 
within Marston Moretaine.

6/7 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
 
24. Mr Van Loen presented 15 five-bedroom detached properties within or near Marston 
Moretaine that had been reduced from band G to band F following the decision concerning 
12 Caves Gardens. Most measured between 206m² and 214m² and all but one benefited 
from a double garage. The Peartrees was larger, at 265m², but was subject to an agricultural 
occupancy restriction. The panel recognised that this restriction affected its value and 
reduced its usefulness as a direct comparison. The Peartrees demonstrated that a dwelling 
larger than the appeal properties could be placed in band F. However, because its 
agricultural occupancy restriction reduced its value, the panel did not regard it as reliable 
evidence that an unrestricted property of the same size should also be placed in band F. 
 
25. Mr Van Loen also relied upon four more five-bedroom detached houses in band F, with three 
bathrooms and floor areas between 213m² and 256m². The panel considered Kingfisher 
House, 151a Bedford Road and Thirsk House to be less reliable comparable properties 
because they were older, non-estate dwellings constructed in the 1920s and 1930s, rather 
than modern estate houses similar to the appeal properties. The remaining properties were 
generally closer to the appeal properties in age, character, accommodation and locality. 
Although many were smaller, they provided a similar level of family accommodation and 
supported the appellants’ contention that properties of this type could properly fall within 
band F. 
 
26. Mr Snell submitted that, apart from 8 Huckle Green, none of the comparable properties relied 
upon by Mr Van Loen exceeded 220m². The panel accepted that many of the appellant’s 
comparable properties were smaller than the appeal properties. However, it was not 
presented with evidence demonstrating that 220m² represented a recognised upper limit for 
band F dwellings, or that a property exceeding that area would necessarily fall within band G. 
The panel therefore treated size as one relevant valuation factor among several, rather than 
as a determining factor. 
 
27. The panel also considered the properties of similar size relied upon by the LO. These 
included 21 Great Blakelands at 227m², 27 Busby Mead and the two Harrison Meadow 
properties at 237m², and 17 Great Blakelands at 257m². They were all five-bedroom 
detached houses with three bathrooms and double garages and were within 0.79 miles of the 
relevant appeal properties. However, all were themselves among the properties under 
appeal. Their band G entries were the subject of the present appeals and could not provide 
independent evidence of a settled band G tone. In addition, earlier proposals concerning 27 
Busby Mead and 17 Great Blakelands had been determined by the LO without further 
appeals, rather than agreed between the parties or determined by a Tribunal. The panel 
found that these entries provided some support for band G, but attached less weight to them 
than to the Tribunal decisions and the subsequent settled reductions relied upon by Mr Van 
Loen. 
 
28. The panel acknowledged that 17 Great Blakelands was larger than the other appeal 
properties. However, even allowing for the extension, the panel was not satisfied that the 
evidence demonstrated a value sufficiently above the remaining dwellings to justify a different 
valuation band. The panel therefore reached the same conclusion for that property as for the 
remaining appeals. 
 
29. Taking the evidence as a whole, the panel found that the established tone of the list, 
supported by the decisions concerning 8 Huckle Green and 12 Caves Gardens and the 
subsequent reductions of similar dwellings within Marston Moretaine, provided the more 
persuasive indication of the correct banding. Although the LO’s sales evidence carried some

weight, it did not enable the panel reliably to conclude that the appeal properties would have 
exceeded £160,000 on 1 April 1991. The panel was not persuaded that the differences in 
size between the band F properties and the appeal dwellings were sufficient to justify band 
G. It therefore concluded that each appeal property would have had an antecedent value 
within the band F range. 
 
Conclusion 
 
30. In view of the above findings and conclusions, the panel therefore allowed the appeals.  
 
Order 
 
31. Under the provisions of regulation 38(2) of the Valuation Tribunal for England (Council Tax 
and Rating Appeals) (Procedure) Regulations 2009, the Valuation Tribunal for England 
orders the LO to reduce the entries in respect of the nine appeal properties from band G to 
band F with effect from their respective relevant dates. 
 
Right of further appeal 
 
32. Any party who is aggrieved at the Tribunal’s decision has a statutory right of further appeal to 
the High Court on a point of law pursuant to Regulation 43 of the Tribunal Procedure 
Regulations. A party does not require permission to appeal from the Tribunal. Any appeal 
must be made directly to the High Court using Form N161 (Appellant’s Notice) within four 
weeks of the date this decision and statement of reasons was issued. 
 
33. Further information regarding this statutory right of further appeal, and the parties’ other 
rights, is contained in the guidance booklet “A guide to tribunal decisions” available on the 
Tribunal’s website at www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk/guidance-booklets/.

24. Mr Van Loen presented 15 five-bedroom detached properties within or near Marston 
Moretaine that had been reduced from band G to band F following the decision concerning

reduced its usefulness as a direct comparison. The Peartrees demonstrated that a dwelling 
larger than the appeal properties could be placed in band F. However, because its 
agricultural occupancy restriction reduced its value, the panel did not regard it as reliable

generally closer to the appeal properties in age, character, accommodation and locality.

supported the appellants’ contention that properties of this type could properly fall within 
band F. 
 
26. Mr Snell submitted that, apart from 8 Huckle Green, none of the comparable properties relied

independent evidence of a settled band G tone. In addition, earlier proposals concerning 27

appeals, rather than agreed between the parties or determined by a Tribunal. The panel

Loen.

evidence demonstrated a value sufficiently above the remaining dwellings to justify a different

subsequent reductions of similar dwellings within Marston Moretaine, provided the more

1.

2.

Introduction 
 
3.

representative.

11. The appeal properties were all five-bedroom detached houses in Marston Moretaine built by

suite shower rooms and a family bathroom on the first floor. Numbers 6 Little Blakelands, 10

were constructed later, between 2018 and 2024. Number 17 Great Blakelands was originally

reception room, giving it four living rooms rather than three. All nine properties also benefited 
from double garages. 
 
12. The panel was, in essence, required to consider the open market value of the properties as 
at 1 April 1991 and considered that the best evidence was to be found in the sales of similar 
properties in the locality close to the valuation date. This baseline date is established by 
legislation and is applicable to all properties, including those that have been built after that 
date.  
 
13. None of the appeal properties were in existence on 1 April 1991. Therefore, it was

which had sold around 1991. The closer the properties were in terms of size, location and 
accommodation, the better the evidence.

142m² and 179m² and sold for values towards the upper end of band F within a year of the

between 2 and 3 miles from the appeal properties. The panel considered that they were too 
far from the appeal properties to provide reliable evidence of values within Marston 
Moretaine and it therefore placed little weight upon them.

properties were within Marston Moretaine and had sold close to 1 April 1991. They were four-
bedroom detached houses measuring 151m². Number 3 sold for £148,000 in September

December 1991. The parties agreed that these sales showed a fall in the market between 
late 1990 and late 1991. They also broadly agreed that the evidence indicated a value in the 
region of £138,000 to £140,000 at the antecedent valuation date. The panel noted that the 
two higher sales occurred before the market had fallen to the level shown by the December 
1991 sale.

parties, or determined by a tribunal panel, were also instrumental in establishing the tone.

reasonable to place some reliance on this evidence.

band G to band F. The panel also noted that it had virtually the same level of accommodation 
and was the same size as five of the appeal properties.

October 2024 concerning 12 Caves Gardens, Marston Moretaine MK43 0TP (VT00020674). 
That property was a five-bedroom detached house measuring 213m², with a double garage, 
and its entry had been reduced from band G to band F. 
 
23. The panel was aware that previous Valuation Tribunal decisions were not binding upon it, but 
they could assist in determining the value or tone of properties within the same locality. Both 
decisions concerned modern five-bedroom detached houses within Marston Moretaine and 
therefore carried significant persuasive weight. The panel also noted that, following the 
decision concerning 12 Caves Gardens, the LO had reduced a substantial number of other 
properties from band G to band F. Those reductions contributed to the current tone of the list 
within Marston Moretaine.

included 21 Great Blakelands at 227m², 27 Busby Mead and the two Harrison Meadow 
properties at 237m², and 17 Great Blakelands at 257m². They were all five-bedroom 
detached houses with three bathrooms and double garages and were within 0.79 miles of the 
relevant appeal properties. However, all were themselves among the properties under 
appeal. Their band G entries were the subject of the present appeals and could not provide 
independent evidence of a settled band G tone. In addition, earlier proposals concerning 27 
Busby Mead and 17 Great Blakelands had been determined by the LO without further 
appeals, rather than agreed between the parties or determined by a Tribunal. The panel

supported by the decisions concerning 8 Huckle Green and 12 Caves Gardens and the

appeal. Their band G entries were the subject of the present appeals and could not provide

DECISION 
 
1.

should be reduced from band G to band F with effect from their respective dates of entry into

Introduction 
 
3.

Listing Officer (LO) on the basis that the entries for each property did not take into account a 
relevant decision of a local Valuation Tribunal, namely the decision dated 16 October 2024 in 
respect of 12 Caves Gardens, MK43 0TP (VT00020674). In making the proposals, the 
appellants sought a reduction in the valuation list entry from band G to band F. After 
considering the merits of the proposals, the LO determined that they were not well founded 
and decision notices to this effect were issued on 23 January 2026.

England under regulation 10 of the Council Tax (Alteration of Lists and Appeals) (England) 
Regulations 2009.

together as they raised substantially the same valuation issues and relied on largely identical 
evidence. Prior to the hearing, the LO filed joint evidence bundles in respect of the nine 
appeals, containing contributions from the appellants and the LO, as required by the 
Tribunal’s standard directions. The LO also stated that copies of the judgments of Domblides 
v Listing Officer [2008] EWHC 3271 (Admin) and Ladies Hosiery & Underwear Ltd v 
Middlesex Assessment Committee (1932) had been provided to the appellants’ 
representative. 
 
6.

proceedings.

7.

8.

1992 No. 550) sets out the statutory basis for valuing dwellings for the purposes of their entry 
into the valuation list. It provides that, having regard to the statutory assumptions, the value

1991. 
 
9.

which dwellings in England are allocated. The bands provide the 1991 range of values. In 
this case, the appeal properties were entered in valuation band G, which applies to values

above £160,000 but no more than £320,000. The appellants sought reductions to band F, 
which applies to values above £120,000 but no more than £160,000. 
 
10. In deciding the values that would have been achieved on 1 April 1991, consideration had to 
be given to the physical state of the locality and the size, layout and character of the 
dwellings on their respective relevant dates, being the dates on which the appeal properties 
entered the valuation list. 
 
Discussion 
 
11. The appeal properties were all five-bedroom detached houses in Marston Moretaine built by 
David Wilson Homes. Their accommodation comprised a lounge, dining room, study, kitchen 
and family room, utility room and cloakroom on the ground floor, with five bedrooms, two en-
suite shower rooms and a family bathroom on the first floor. Numbers 6 Little Blakelands, 10 
Little Beanhills and 21 Great Blakelands were constructed in 2014 and were the “Manning” 
house type, measuring 227m². The “Glidewell” properties comprised 27 Busby Mead, 11 
Huckle Green, 11 and 15 Harrison Meadow and 5 Harper Grove. They measured 237m² and 
were constructed later, between 2018 and 2024. Number 17 Great Blakelands was originally 
a Manning house but was extended from 227m² to 257m². It contained an additional 
reception room, giving it four living rooms rather than three. All nine properties also benefited 
from double garages. 
 
12. The panel was, in essence, required to consider the open market value of the properties as 
at 1 April 1991 and considered that the best evidence was to be found in the sales of similar 
properties in the locality close to the valuation date. This baseline date is established by 
legislation and is applicable to all properties, including those that have been built after that 
date.  
 
13. None of the appeal properties were in existence on 1 April 1991. Therefore, it was 
reasonable to value them having regard to other detached houses that were comparable and 
which had sold around 1991. The closer the properties were in terms of size, location and 
accommodation, the better the evidence. 
 
14. In support of band G, Mr Snell presented the sales of seven smaller detached houses in 
band F that had sold close to 1 April 1991. Four of those properties measured between 
142m² and 179m² and sold for values towards the upper end of band F within a year of the 
antecedent valuation date. However, they were located in Wootton, Cranfield and Ampthill, 
between 2 and 3 miles from the appeal properties. The panel considered that they were too 
far from the appeal properties to provide reliable evidence of values within Marston 
Moretaine and it therefore placed little weight upon them. 
 
15. The panel attached greater weight to the sales of 3, 11 and 14 Denbigh Close because those 
properties were within Marston Moretaine and had sold close to 1 April 1991. They were four-
bedroom detached houses measuring 151m². Number 3 sold for £148,000 in September 
1990, number 14 sold for £153,500 in September 1990 and number 11 sold for £130,000 in 
December 1991. The parties agreed that these sales showed a fall in the market between 
late 1990 and late 1991. They also broadly agreed that the evidence indicated a value in the 
region of £138,000 to £140,000 at the antecedent valuation date. The panel noted that the 
two higher sales occurred before the market had fallen to the level shown by the December 
1991 sale.

16. The panel accepted that the appeal properties would have been more valuable than the 
Denbigh Close properties. However, it was difficult to determine whether the difference would 
have been sufficient to produce values above £160,000. The Denbigh Close properties 
measured 151m², whereas the appeal properties measured between 227m² and 257m². This 
substantial difference in size made it difficult to make a direct comparison. The panel was not 
persuaded that the difference in floor area, by itself, showed how much more the appeal 
properties would have sold for in 1991. No sale of a similar-sized band G property in Marston 
Moretaine close to 1 April 1991 was presented to confirm that the appeal properties would 
have exceeded the band F upper limit. 
 
17. The LO sought to support its valuation by applying percentage differences in floor area and 
later sale prices to the Denbigh Close evidence. The 2017 sale of 14 Denbigh Close for 
£430,000 was compared with the 2017 sale of 21 Great Blakelands for £590,000 and the LO 
also relied upon the higher later sale prices achieved by other appeal properties. 
 
18. However, the panel was not satisfied that applying a percentage difference in size or later 
sale price to a 1990 or 1991 sale provided a sufficiently reliable valuation method. Size was 
relevant, but it was not the only factor affecting value. The evidence did not establish that the 
same percentage differences would have applied in the local market on 1 April 1991. The 
panel therefore placed some weight upon the LO’s sales evidence but did not consider that it 
established values above £160,000 for the appeal properties. 
 
19. The panel also had regard to the ‘tone’ or pattern of bandings already in the valuation list. A 
tone of band was established when a number of properties, similar in size, character, quality, 
detachment and location were attributed the same level of band which, over time, had not 
been challenged. Council tax bands that had been challenged and subsequently agreed by 
parties, or determined by a tribunal panel, were also instrumental in establishing the tone. 
 
20. When the original valuation list was compiled in 1993, a tone had not been established as 
many of the initial bandings were being challenged.  However, the bands were now in a more 
settled stage in the life of the valuation list after over 30 years of scrutiny. It was therefore 
reasonable to place some reliance on this evidence. 
 
21. To further support the appellants’ case, Mr Van Loen provided the panel with the previous 
Tribunal decision of 8 Huckle Green (VT00012229), which was the relevant decision that 
formed the basis of appeal for 12 Caves Gardens. At 237m², it was also a five-bedroom 
detached house situated within Marston Moretaine, and its entry had been reduced from 
band G to band F. The panel also noted that it had virtually the same level of accommodation 
and was the same size as five of the appeal properties. 
 
22. The proposals giving rise to these appeals were based on the Tribunal decision dated 16 
October 2024 concerning 12 Caves Gardens, Marston Moretaine MK43 0TP (VT00020674). 
That property was a five-bedroom detached house measuring 213m², with a double garage, 
and its entry had been reduced from band G to band F. 
 
23. The panel was aware that previous Valuation Tribunal decisions were not binding upon it, but 
they could assist in determining the value or tone of properties within the same locality. Both 
decisions concerned modern five-bedroom detached houses within Marston Moretaine and 
therefore carried significant persuasive weight. The panel also noted that, following the 
decision concerning 12 Caves Gardens, the LO had reduced a substantial number of other 
properties from band G to band F. Those reductions contributed to the current tone of the list 
within Marston Moretaine.

6/7 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
 
24. Mr Van Loen presented 15 five-bedroom detached properties within or near Marston 
Moretaine that had been reduced from band G to band F following the decision concerning 
12 Caves Gardens. Most measured between 206m² and 214m² and all but one benefited 
from a double garage. The Peartrees was larger, at 265m², but was subject to an agricultural 
occupancy restriction. The panel recognised that this restriction affected its value and 
reduced its usefulness as a direct comparison. The Peartrees demonstrated that a dwelling 
larger than the appeal properties could be placed in band F. However, because its 
agricultural occupancy restriction reduced its value, the panel did not regard it as reliable 
evidence that an unrestricted property of the same size should also be placed in band F. 
 
25. Mr Van Loen also relied upon four more five-bedroom detached houses in band F, with three 
bathrooms and floor areas between 213m² and 256m². The panel considered Kingfisher 
House, 151a Bedford Road and Thirsk House to be less reliable comparable properties 
because they were older, non-estate dwellings constructed in the 1920s and 1930s, rather 
than modern estate houses similar to the appeal properties. The remaining properties were 
generally closer to the appeal properties in age, character, accommodation and locality. 
Although many were smaller, they provided a similar level of family accommodation and 
supported the appellants’ contention that properties of this type could properly fall within 
band F. 
 
26. Mr Snell submitted that, apart from 8 Huckle Green, none of the comparable properties relied 
upon by Mr Van Loen exceeded 220m². The panel accepted that many of the appellant’s 
comparable properties were smaller than the appeal properties. However, it was not 
presented with evidence demonstrating that 220m² represented a recognised upper limit for 
band F dwellings, or that a property exceeding that area would necessarily fall within band G. 
The panel therefore treated size as one relevant valuation factor among several, rather than 
as a determining factor. 
 
27. The panel also considered the properties of similar size relied upon by the LO. These 
included 21 Great Blakelands at 227m², 27 Busby Mead and the two Harrison Meadow 
properties at 237m², and 17 Great Blakelands at 257m². They were all five-bedroom 
detached houses with three bathrooms and double garages and were within 0.79 miles of the 
relevant appeal properties. However, all were themselves among the properties under 
appeal. Their band G entries were the subject of the present appeals and could not provide 
independent evidence of a settled band G tone. In addition, earlier proposals concerning 27 
Busby Mead and 17 Great Blakelands had been determined by the LO without further 
appeals, rather than agreed between the parties or determined by a Tribunal. The panel 
found that these entries provided some support for band G, but attached less weight to them 
than to the Tribunal decisions and the subsequent settled reductions relied upon by Mr Van 
Loen. 
 
28. The panel acknowledged that 17 Great Blakelands was larger than the other appeal 
properties. However, even allowing for the extension, the panel was not satisfied that the 
evidence demonstrated a value sufficiently above the remaining dwellings to justify a different 
valuation band. The panel therefore reached the same conclusion for that property as for the 
remaining appeals. 
 
29. Taking the evidence as a whole, the panel found that the established tone of the list, 
supported by the decisions concerning 8 Huckle Green and 12 Caves Gardens and the 
subsequent reductions of similar dwellings within Marston Moretaine, provided the more 
persuasive indication of the correct banding. Although the LO’s sales evidence carried some

weight, it did not enable the panel reliably to conclude that the appeal properties would have 
exceeded £160,000 on 1 April 1991. The panel was not persuaded that the differences in 
size between the band F properties and the appeal dwellings were sufficient to justify band 
G. It therefore concluded that each appeal property would have had an antecedent value 
within the band F range. 
 
Conclusion 
 
30. In view of the above findings and conclusions, the panel therefore allowed the appeals.  
 
Order 
 
31. Under the provisions of regulation 38(2) of the Valuation Tribunal for England (Council Tax 
and Rating Appeals) (Procedure) Regulations 2009, the Valuation Tribunal for England 
orders the LO to reduce the entries in respect of the nine appeal properties from band G to 
band F with effect from their respective relevant dates.

32. Any party who is aggrieved at the Tribunal’s decision has a statutory right of further appeal to 
the High Court on a point of law pursuant to Regulation 43 of the Tribunal Procedure 
Regulations. A party does not require permission to appeal from the Tribunal. Any appeal 
must be made directly to the High Court using Form N161 (Appellant’s Notice) within four

rights, is contained in the guidance booklet “A guide to tribunal decisions” available on the

1. 
The appeals are allowed.  
 
2. 
The panel determined that the council tax valuation list entries for the appeal properties 
should be reduced from band G to band F with effect from their respective dates of entry into 
the council tax list, as set out in the Schedule on page two. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
On 29 and 30 April 2025, Mr Van Loen, on behalf of the appellants, served proposals on the

appellants sought a reduction in the valuation list entry from band G to band F. After 
considering the merits of the proposals, the LO determined that they were not well founded

4.

5.

v Listing Officer [2008] EWHC 3271 (Admin) and Ladies Hosiery & Underwear Ltd v 
Middlesex Assessment Committee (1932) had been provided to the appellants’ 
representative. 
 
6.

proceedings.

7.

into the valuation list. It provides that, having regard to the statutory assumptions, the value 
of any dwelling, shall be taken to be the amount it would reasonably expect to realise had it 
been sold in an open market by a willing vendor, on the antecedent valuation date of 1 April 
1991.

which dwellings in England are allocated. The bands provide the 1991 range of values. In 
this case, the appeal properties were entered in valuation band G, which applies to values

be given to the physical state of the locality and the size, layout and character of the 
dwellings on their respective relevant dates, being the dates on which the appeal properties 
entered the valuation list.

11. The appeal properties were all five-bedroom detached houses in Marston Moretaine built by 
David Wilson Homes. Their accommodation comprised a lounge, dining room, study, kitchen 
and family room, utility room and cloakroom on the ground floor, with five bedrooms, two en-
suite shower rooms and a family bathroom on the first floor. Numbers 6 Little Blakelands, 10 
Little Beanhills and 21 Great Blakelands were constructed in 2014 and were the “Manning”

Huckle Green, 11 and 15 Harrison Meadow and 5 Harper Grove. They measured 237m² and

a Manning house but was extended from 227m² to 257m². It contained an additional 
reception room, giving it four living rooms rather than three. All nine properties also benefited 
from double garages.

date.

which had sold around 1991. The closer the properties were in terms of size, location and 
accommodation, the better the evidence.

between 2 and 3 miles from the appeal properties. The panel considered that they were too 
far from the appeal properties to provide reliable evidence of values within Marston 
Moretaine and it therefore placed little weight upon them.

1991 sale.

Moretaine close to 1 April 1991 was presented to confirm that the appeal properties would 
have exceeded the band F upper limit.

been challenged. Council tax bands that had been challenged and subsequently agreed by 
parties, or determined by a tribunal panel, were also instrumental in establishing the tone. 
 
20. When the original valuation list was compiled in 1993, a tone had not been established as

settled stage in the life of the valuation list after over 30 years of scrutiny. It was therefore

and its entry had been reduced from band G to band F.

they could assist in determining the value or tone of properties within the same locality. Both 
decisions concerned modern five-bedroom detached houses within Marston Moretaine and 
therefore carried significant persuasive weight. The panel also noted that, following the 
decision concerning 12 Caves Gardens, the LO had reduced a substantial number of other 
properties from band G to band F. Those reductions contributed to the current tone of the list 
within Marston Moretaine.

Moretaine that had been reduced from band G to band F following the decision concerning

generally closer to the appeal properties in age, character, accommodation and locality. 
Although many were smaller, they provided a similar level of family accommodation and 
supported the appellants’ contention that properties of this type could properly fall within 
band F. 
 
26. Mr Snell submitted that, apart from 8 Huckle Green, none of the comparable properties relied 
upon by Mr Van Loen exceeded 220m². The panel accepted that many of the appellant’s 
comparable properties were smaller than the appeal properties. However, it was not 
presented with evidence demonstrating that 220m² represented a recognised upper limit for 
band F dwellings, or that a property exceeding that area would necessarily fall within band G. 
The panel therefore treated size as one relevant valuation factor among several, rather than 
as a determining factor. 
 
27. The panel also considered the properties of similar size relied upon by the LO. These 
included 21 Great Blakelands at 227m², 27 Busby Mead and the two Harrison Meadow 
properties at 237m², and 17 Great Blakelands at 257m². They were all five-bedroom 
detached houses with three bathrooms and double garages and were within 0.79 miles of the 
relevant appeal properties. However, all were themselves among the properties under 
appeal. Their band G entries were the subject of the present appeals and could not provide 
independent evidence of a settled band G tone. In addition, earlier proposals concerning 27 
Busby Mead and 17 Great Blakelands had been determined by the LO without further 
appeals, rather than agreed between the parties or determined by a Tribunal. The panel 
found that these entries provided some support for band G, but attached less weight to them 
than to the Tribunal decisions and the subsequent settled reductions relied upon by Mr Van 
Loen. 
 
28. The panel acknowledged that 17 Great Blakelands was larger than the other appeal 
properties. However, even allowing for the extension, the panel was not satisfied that the 
evidence demonstrated a value sufficiently above the remaining dwellings to justify a different 
valuation band. The panel therefore reached the same conclusion for that property as for the 
remaining appeals. 
 
29. Taking the evidence as a whole, the panel found that the established tone of the list, 
supported by the decisions concerning 8 Huckle Green and 12 Caves Gardens and the 
subsequent reductions of similar dwellings within Marston Moretaine, provided the more 
persuasive indication of the correct banding. Although the LO’s sales evidence carried some

G. It therefore concluded that each appeal property would have had an antecedent value

30. In view of the above findings and conclusions, the panel therefore allowed the appeals.

December 1991. The parties agreed that these sales showed a fall in the market between 
late 1990 and late 1991. They also broadly agreed that the evidence indicated a value in the 
region of £138,000 to £140,000 at the antecedent valuation date. The panel noted that the 
two higher sales occurred before the market had fallen to the level shown by the December 
1991 sale.

D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
5/7 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
16. The panel accepted that the appeal properties would have been more valuable than the 
Denbigh Close properties. However, it was difficult to determine whether the difference would 
have been sufficient to produce values above £160,000. The Denbigh Close properties 
measured 151m², whereas the appeal properties measured between 227m² and 257m². This 
substantial difference in size made it difficult to make a direct comparison. The panel was not 
persuaded that the difference in floor area, by itself, showed how much more the appeal 
properties would have sold for in 1991. No sale of a similar-sized band G property in Marston 
Moretaine close to 1 April 1991 was presented to confirm that the appeal properties would 
have exceeded the band F upper limit. 
 
17. The LO sought to support its valuation by applying percentage differences in floor area and 
later sale prices to the Denbigh Close evidence. The 2017 sale of 14 Denbigh Close for 
£430,000 was compared with the 2017 sale of 21 Great Blakelands for £590,000 and the LO 
also relied upon the higher later sale prices achieved by other appeal properties. 
 
18. However, the panel was not satisfied that applying a percentage difference in size or later 
sale price to a 1990 or 1991 sale provided a sufficiently reliable valuation method. Size was 
relevant, but it was not the only factor affecting value. The evidence did not establish that the 
same percentage differences would have applied in the local market on 1 April 1991. The 
panel therefore placed some weight upon the LO’s sales evidence but did not consider that it 
established values above £160,000 for the appeal properties. 
 
19. The panel also had regard to the ‘tone’ or pattern of bandings already in the valuation list. A 
tone of band was established when a number of properties, similar in size, character, quality, 
detachment and location were attributed the same level of band which, over time, had not 
been challenged. Council tax bands that had been challenged and subsequently agreed by 
parties, or determined by a tribunal panel, were also instrumental in establishing the tone. 
 
20. When the original valuation list was compiled in 1993, a tone had not been established as 
many of the initial bandings were being challenged.  However, the bands were now in a more 
settled stage in the life of the valuation list after over 30 years of scrutiny. It was therefore 
reasonable to place some reliance on this evidence. 
 
21. To further support the appellants’ case, Mr Van Loen provided the panel with the previous 
Tribunal decision of 8 Huckle Green (VT00012229), which was the relevant decision that 
formed the basis of appeal for 12 Caves Gardens. At 237m², it was also a five-bedroom 
detached house situated within Marston Moretaine, and its entry had been reduced from 
band G to band F. The panel also noted that it had virtually the same level of accommodation 
and was the same size as five of the appeal properties. 
 
22. The proposals giving rise to these appeals were based on the Tribunal decision dated 16 
October 2024 concerning 12 Caves Gardens, Marston Moretaine MK43 0TP (VT00020674). 
That property was a five-bedroom detached house measuring 213m², with a double garage, 
and its entry had been reduced from band G to band F. 
 
23. The panel was aware that previous Valuation Tribunal decisions were not binding upon it, but 
they could assist in determining the value or tone of properties within the same locality. Both 
decisions concerned modern five-bedroom detached houses within Marston Moretaine and 
therefore carried significant persuasive weight. The panel also noted that, following the 
decision concerning 12 Caves Gardens, the LO had reduced a substantial number of other 
properties from band G to band F. Those reductions contributed to the current tone of the list 
within Marston Moretaine. 

[2026] VTE VT00036172 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
6/7 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
 
24. Mr Van Loen presented 15 five-bedroom detached properties within or near Marston 
Moretaine that had been reduced from band G to band F following the decision concerning 
12 Caves Gardens. Most measured between 206m² and 214m² and all but one benefited 
from a double garage. The Peartrees was larger, at 265m², but was subject to an agricultural 
occupancy restriction. The panel recognised that this restriction affected its value and 
reduced its usefulness as a direct comparison. The Peartrees demonstrated that a dwelling 
larger than the appeal properties could be placed in band F. However, because its 
agricultural occupancy restriction reduced its value, the panel did not regard it as reliable 
evidence that an unrestricted property of the same size should also be placed in band F. 
 
25. Mr Van Loen also relied upon four more five-bedroom detached houses in band F, with three 
bathrooms and floor areas between 213m² and 256m². The panel considered Kingfisher 
House, 151a Bedford Road and Thirsk House to be less reliable comparable properties 
because they were older, non-estate dwellings constructed in the 1920s and 1930s, rather 
than modern estate houses similar to the appeal properties. The remaining properties were 
generally closer to the appeal properties in age, character, accommodation and locality. 
Although many were smaller, they provided a similar level of family accommodation and 
supported the appellants’ contention that properties of this type could properly fall within 
band F. 
 
26. Mr Snell submitted that, apart from 8 Huckle Green, none of the comparable properties relied 
upon by Mr Van Loen exceeded 220m². The panel accepted that many of the appellant’s 
comparable properties were smaller than the appeal properties. However, it was not 
presented with evidence demonstrating that 220m² represented a recognised upper limit for 
band F dwellings, or that a property exceeding that area would necessarily fall within band G. 
The panel therefore treated size as one relevant valuation factor among several, rather than 
as a determining factor. 
 
27. The panel also considered the properties of similar size relied upon by the LO. These 
included 21 Great Blakelands at 227m², 27 Busby Mead and the two Harrison Meadow 
properties at 237m², and 17 Great Blakelands at 257m². They were all five-bedroom 
detached houses with three bathrooms and double garages and were within 0.79 miles of the 
relevant appeal properties. However, all were themselves among the properties under 
appeal. Their band G entries were the subject of the present appeals and could not provide 
independent evidence of a settled band G tone. In addition, earlier proposals concerning 27 
Busby Mead and 17 Great Blakelands had been determined by the LO without further 
appeals, rather than agreed between the parties or determined by a Tribunal. The panel 
found that these entries provided some support for band G, but attached less weight to them 
than to the Tribunal decisions and the subsequent settled reductions relied upon by Mr Van 
Loen. 
 
28. The panel acknowledged that 17 Great Blakelands was larger than the other appeal 
properties. However, even allowing for the extension, the panel was not satisfied that the 
evidence demonstrated a value sufficiently above the remaining dwellings to justify a different 
valuation band. The panel therefore reached the same conclusion for that property as for the 
remaining appeals. 
 
29. Taking the evidence as a whole, the panel found that the established tone of the list, 
supported by the decisions concerning 8 Huckle Green and 12 Caves Gardens and the 
subsequent reductions of similar dwellings within Marston Moretaine, provided the more 
persuasive indication of the correct banding. Although the LO’s sales evidence carried some 

[2026] VTE VT00036172 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
7/7 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
weight, it did not enable the panel reliably to conclude that the appeal properties would have 
exceeded £160,000 on 1 April 1991. The panel was not persuaded that the differences in 
size between the band F properties and the appeal dwellings were sufficient to justify band 
G. It therefore concluded that each appeal property would have had an antecedent value 
within the band F range. 
 
Conclusion 
 
30. In view of the above findings and conclusions, the panel therefore allowed the appeals.  
 
Order 
 
31. Under the provisions of regulation 38(2) of the Valuation Tribunal for England (Council Tax 
and Rating Appeals) (Procedure) Regulations 2009, the Valuation Tribunal for England 
orders the LO to reduce the entries in respect of the nine appeal properties from band G to 
band F with effect from their respective relevant dates.

Decision 
1. The appeals are dismissed. 
 
2. I found that the subject properties were hereditaments, and therefore dwellings, on the 
proposed effective date of 1 April 2025. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. The appeal process began when the appellant served proposals on the Listing Officer (LO) at 
the Valuation Office. The appellant made the proposals to have the subject properties deleted 
from the valuation list with effect from 1 April 2025. The LO issued her decisions in respect of 
the proposals on 29 September 2025, and these were challenged by way of appeals to the 
Valuation Tribunal on 28 December 2025. 
 
4. Within 24 hours of the hearing, one of the panel members advised they were no longer able to 
sit that day due to unforeseen circumstances. The Tribunal business arrangements provide 
that a Senior Member of the Tribunal may sit alone. I am therefore satisfied that I was 
authorised to hear and determine this appeal sitting alone.  
 
5. With the agreement of the parties, the panel varied the procedure outlined in the Consolidated 
Practice Statement PS8 – Model Procedure and invited the respondent to present her 
evidence first. 
 
6. This statement of reasons is not and does not purport to be a full verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Background 
 
7. The subject properties were three converted flats within one house. The properties were left to 
the appellant when his brother passed away. The properties had not been maintained for the 
previous 12 years prior to the appellant taking ownership. He was seeking deletion from 1 April 
2025 which is when he was able to provide photographic evidence from. He sought deletion 
on the basis the properties were derelict and beyond reasonable repair. 
 
8. The following case law was referred to at the hearing: 
 
• Wilson v Coll (Listing Officer) [2011] EWHC 2824 (Admin) 
• Newbigin (Valuation Officer) v S J & J Monk [2017] UKSC 14 
• Bunyan (Listing Officer) v Patel [2022] EWHC 1143 (Admin) 
Relevant Law 
 
The Local Government Finance Act 1992 
 
9. The legal basis of a dwelling for council tax purposes is that it must constitute a hereditament, 
in accordance with section 3 to the Local Government Finance Act 1992:   
 
“Meaning of “dwelling” 
3(1) This section has effect for determining what is a dwelling for the purposes of this Part. 

[2026] VTE VT00034454 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
3/5 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
 
3(2) Subject to the following provisions of this section, a dwelling is any property which – 
 
(a) by virtue of the definition of hereditament in section 115(1) of the General Rate Act 
1967, would have been a hereditament for the purposes of that Act if that Act 
remained in force; and 
 
(b) is not for the time being shown or required to be shown in a local or a central non-
domestic rating list in force at that time;” 
 
10. Section 115(1) of the General Rate Act 1967 defined a hereditament as: 
 
“property which is, or may be liable to a rate, being a unit of such property which is, or would 
fall to be shown as a separate item in the Valuation List.” 
 
11. A dwelling within the meaning of section 3, is a unit of property that qualifies as a hereditament 
because it is capable of beneficial occupation and is domestic property.  
 
Discussion 
 
12. The issue before me was to determine whether the properties should be deleted from the 
valuation list with effect from 1 April 2025, the date proposed by the appellant. Therefore, I 
must consider the physical state of the subject properties on that proposed effective date. 
 
13. The correct approach in appeals of this nature is to consider whether a hereditament exists at 
the proposed effective date. If it does, then it must be valued on the statutory assumption that 
it is in reasonable repair even if, in reality, it is in need of repair. 
 
14. In Wilson v Coll, the appeal property was generally in a poor condition, but capable of being 
repaired. In the judgement a distinction was drawn between the appeal property and one that 
was “truly derelict”. If a property was “truly derelict”, it would fail to be a hereditament and so 
not appear in the council tax list.  
 
15. In Newbigin v Monk, a non-domestic rating case, the Supreme Court decided that a property 
which was incapable of beneficial occupation due to a scheme of works was not a 
hereditament. In the subject appeal, there was no evidence of a scheme of works on the 
proposed effective date of 1 April 2025, or that any works had started at this point. The 
appellant stated at the hearing that works had not commenced, however they would be 
commencing imminently. 
 
16. In Bunyan v Patel, a council tax deletion appeal, the High Court considered whether the 
appeal property should be deleted from the valuation list. In that case, the landlord sought a 
deletion for poor repair the day after the tenant left the appeal property. The LO accepted that, 
about a year later, there was a scheme of works underway and those works were significant 
and would change the character of the property. The judge reviewed Wilson v Coll as well as 
Monk and concluded that the LO’s approach as set out in the Council Tax Manual was correct.  
 
17. I heard from Miss Portman that the external photographs provided showed that the overall 
structure appeared sound. She referred to a report from the local authority inspector who had 
visited the properties on 15 December 2025 which stated that there was no evidence the main 
structure was unsound. 
 

[2026] VTE VT00034454 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
4/5 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
18. Miss Portman stated that the list of works provided by the appellant was renovation works 
which had not begun. She did state that once the works began, the properties may qualify to 
be removed from the valuation list. This was not for me to consider at this hearing as it was an 
event which had not yet commenced. 
 
19. I heard from the appellant that it was his contention that the case law that had been referred to 
was nonsense and did not apply. He found it hard to fathom that there was no economic test 
to be considered. He argued that the cost to reinstate all three properties to a habitable 
condition would cost approximately £234,000. This was evidenced by the builder’s quote, 
however he stated this could increase if further works were discovered during the process. 
The appellant’s view was that the properties were beyond ‘reasonable repair’ at the proposed 
effective date and that the physical works required consisted of major replacement and 
reconstruction meant they were no longer dwellings. 
 
20. Through questioning I established that the hole in the roof the appellant had referred to was 
the plastic corrugated roof of the conservatory and that this was not built to the same standard 
as the main house. The appellant stated that there was no electrics, gas or water at the 
properties as the services had been turned off, however, he was unable to confirm if any pipes 
were removed or if there were services to the plot.  
 
21. I reviewed the photographs in the evidence bundle and the appellant assisted me by 
describing which flat each photograph was of. I accepted that the property was in poor repair. 
The appellant explained that vandals had been in the property and destroyed toilets and 
shattered the glass from some windows. The properties had been left with a significant amount 
of rubbish, holes had been made in some walls, and a significant amount of cleaning would be 
required. 
 
22. I acknowledged the appellant’s view of the case law; however, I am bound by the case law 
and the legislation in place when considering these appeals. No evidence had been provided 
to demonstrate that the properties were structurally unsound. I was of the view that the 
conservatory was not part of the main house when considering whether it was wind or 
watertight. The conservatory was made from inferior materials such as a corrugated plastic 
roof and was attached to the exterior brick wall of the house.  
 
23. I considered the case law before me and found that Monk v Newbigin did not apply in this 
case as there was no schedule of works currently taking place. The appellant confirmed at the 
hearing that there were currently no works taking place. Therefore, I had to consider whether, 
‘having regard to the character of the property and a reasonable amount of repair works being 
undertaken could the premises be occupied as a dwelling?’. This was identified as the correct 
test in Wilson v Coll and confirmed in Bunyan v Patel. 
 
24. The appellant stated that the subject property was uninhabitable. While I acknowledged that 
someone would not want to live in the subject property in its current state, when deciding this 
appeal, I was bound by the appropriate law which in this case is the Local Government 
Finance Act. The test is whether it was capable of repair and therefore remained a 
hereditament. 
 
25. Based on the evidence before me, both in the evidence bundle and the verbal evidence at the 
hearing, I am satisfied that the subject properties remained hereditaments and that the 
properties were not truly derelict. The evidence supported that the properties could be 
repaired. When considering reasonable repair, I am aware that Wilson v Coll established there 
was no economical test within the legislation for residential dwellings, however it would be 

[2026] VTE VT00034454 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
5/5 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
appropriate for me to consider the term reasonable. It is my view that the repair work required 
for the properties to be occupied as dwellings was reasonable. The cost of £234,000 listed in 
the quote provided by the builder was less than half of the value of the whole property in good 
condition, which the appellant had stated was £500,000 to £600,000. Therefore, I found that it 
would be reasonable for the repair work to be carried out on that basis. 
 
Conclusion 
 
26. In view of the above findings and conclusions, I was satisfied that the subject properties 
remained hereditaments, and therefore dwellings, on 1 April 2025, and therefore the appeals 
were dismissed.

27. Any party who is aggrieved at the Tribunal’s decision has a statutory right of further appeal to

was “truly derelict”. If a property was “truly derelict”, it would fail to be a hereditament and so 
not appear in the council tax list.  
 
15. In Newbigin v Monk, a non-domestic rating case, the Supreme Court decided that a property 
which was incapable of beneficial occupation due to a scheme of works was not a 
hereditament. In the subject appeal, there was no evidence of a scheme of works on the 
proposed effective date of 1 April 2025, or that any works had started at this point. The 
appellant stated at the hearing that works had not commenced, however they would be 
commencing imminently. 
 
16. In Bunyan v Patel, a council tax deletion appeal, the High Court considered whether the 
appeal property should be deleted from the valuation list. In that case, the landlord sought a 
deletion for poor repair the day after the tenant left the appeal property. The LO accepted that, 
about a year later, there was a scheme of works underway and those works were significant 
and would change the character of the property. The judge reviewed Wilson v Coll as well as 
Monk and concluded that the LO’s approach as set out in the Council Tax Manual was correct.  
 
17. I heard from Miss Portman that the external photographs provided showed that the overall 
structure appeared sound. She referred to a report from the local authority inspector who had 
visited the properties on 15 December 2025 which stated that there was no evidence the main 
structure was unsound.

18. Miss Portman stated that the list of works provided by the appellant was renovation works 
which had not begun. She did state that once the works began, the properties may qualify to 
be removed from the valuation list. This was not for me to consider at this hearing as it was an 
event which had not yet commenced. 
 
19. I heard from the appellant that it was his contention that the case law that had been referred to 
was nonsense and did not apply. He found it hard to fathom that there was no economic test 
to be considered. He argued that the cost to reinstate all three properties to a habitable 
condition would cost approximately £234,000. This was evidenced by the builder’s quote, 
however he stated this could increase if further works were discovered during the process. 
The appellant’s view was that the properties were beyond ‘reasonable repair’ at the proposed 
effective date and that the physical works required consisted of major replacement and 
reconstruction meant they were no longer dwellings. 
 
20. Through questioning I established that the hole in the roof the appellant had referred to was 
the plastic corrugated roof of the conservatory and that this was not built to the same standard 
as the main house. The appellant stated that there was no electrics, gas or water at the 
properties as the services had been turned off, however, he was unable to confirm if any pipes 
were removed or if there were services to the plot.  
 
21. I reviewed the photographs in the evidence bundle and the appellant assisted me by 
describing which flat each photograph was of. I accepted that the property was in poor repair. 
The appellant explained that vandals had been in the property and destroyed toilets and 
shattered the glass from some windows. The properties had been left with a significant amount 
of rubbish, holes had been made in some walls, and a significant amount of cleaning would be 
required. 
 
22. I acknowledged the appellant’s view of the case law; however, I am bound by the case law 
and the legislation in place when considering these appeals. No evidence had been provided 
to demonstrate that the properties were structurally unsound. I was of the view that the 
conservatory was not part of the main house when considering whether it was wind or 
watertight. The conservatory was made from inferior materials such as a corrugated plastic 
roof and was attached to the exterior brick wall of the house.  
 
23. I considered the case law before me and found that Monk v Newbigin did not apply in this 
case as there was no schedule of works currently taking place. The appellant confirmed at the 
hearing that there were currently no works taking place. Therefore, I had to consider whether, 
‘having regard to the character of the property and a reasonable amount of repair works being 
undertaken could the premises be occupied as a dwelling?’. This was identified as the correct 
test in Wilson v Coll and confirmed in Bunyan v Patel. 
 
24. The appellant stated that the subject property was uninhabitable. While I acknowledged that 
someone would not want to live in the subject property in its current state, when deciding this 
appeal, I was bound by the appropriate law which in this case is the Local Government 
Finance Act. The test is whether it was capable of repair and therefore remained a 
hereditament. 
 
25. Based on the evidence before me, both in the evidence bundle and the verbal evidence at the 
hearing, I am satisfied that the subject properties remained hereditaments and that the 
properties were not truly derelict. The evidence supported that the properties could be 
repaired. When considering reasonable repair, I am aware that Wilson v Coll established there 
was no economical test within the legislation for residential dwellings, however it would be

26. In view of the above findings and conclusions, I was satisfied that the subject properties
